responses_archetypeVariants.sophisticate: The sophisticate version is not naive techno-utopianism; it is a discounting argument. Suffering, he says, is a solvable engineering problem, and once that trajectory is granted, present procreation is justified as the cost of arriving — the early generations are the price of the cure. Grant the trajectory arguendo. Grant that descendants centuries out suffer far less. The case still fails, and on the project's own spine, because the asymmetry does not run through the people who will benefit. The beings created now bear one hundred percent of present conditions — disease, decline, the full existential load, death — and they are non-consenting transitional sacrifices for a population that does not yet exist and may never. The asymmetry is decisive precisely because suffering-abolition is conceded: had those present beings not been created, the absence of their suffering would be good, while the absence of the speculative future-good they were spent to purchase deprives no one, because there is no one there to be deprived. You cannot net a benefit owed to hypothetical descendants against a harm imposed on actual people who never agreed to fund it. And the deferral itself is the tell. Every generation has been told its suffering was the meaningful down-payment on a better tomorrow; the narrative's function is to convert imposed misery into purpose and so suppress the recognition that consent was never sought. The improvement period is always now and always projected to close just ahead. The empirical record is a secondary point and must not carry the argument, but it is unkind to the optimist: progress is lateral, not directional — the century of antibiotics was equally the century of nuclear weapons and industrial confinement — so the same capacity that might one day reduce suffering reliably manufactures novel forms of it. The trajectory is assumed; the bill is certain; and it is sent to people who never signed for it.
